summary: Defines TLS ciphersuites for certificateless authentication using only a simple, low-entropy password, called TLS-PWD. They use an authentication and key exchange protocol called dragonfly.

eli5.summary: You can log in with just a short password and no ID card, and the password is not exposed to someone listening.

subtitle: Secure TLS authentication using only a password, without certificates.

tldr.problem: TLS normally requires public key certificates for authentication, which are complex to provision and manage. For simple devices and embedded systems, users need to authenticate with a password instead, but naive password-based protocols are vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks.
tldr.mechanism: TLS-PWD defines new TLS ciphersuites based on the dragonfly password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE). Both sides derive a password element from a shared password, prove knowledge of that element through cryptographic commitments, and establish an authenticated session key—all resistant to offline dictionary attacks.
tldr.outcome: Servers and clients can now authenticate with only a low-entropy password, without certificates. The protocol proves knowledge of the password through one-time commitments that cannot be replayed or attacked offline; an attacker gets one guess per active interaction.

today: RFC 8492 is an Informational document published in February 2019. TLS-PWD ciphersuites have been assigned IANA values and are available for implementation. Support in TLS libraries remains limited but the specification is stable and ready for use in applications that require password-only authentication.

sections.title: Why Passwords for TLS Authentication
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the standard for encrypting web and application traffic, but it typically requires public key certificates for authentication. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem: to enroll for a certificate, you need an already-secure channel; but to create that channel, many devices and people need something simpler to provision than certificates.

Many embedded systems, IoT devices, and interactive applications run TLS with self-signed certificates and then do password exchange over the already-encrypted channel—a workaround that works but is inelegant and not formally specified. TLS-PWD defines a clean alternative: the ability to authenticate using only a password, without ever needing a certificate. The protocol is resistant to dictionary attacks, meaning an attacker cannot take a password list offline and try them against a recorded handshake. Each guess requires an active interaction with the server.
sections.eli5: Some devices don't need fancy ID cards. TLS-PWD lets them just use a password, and makes sure no one can steal it by trying lots of guesses without actually talking to the device.

sections.title: The Dragonfly Protocol
sections.content:
TLS-PWD is built on the dragonfly password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) protocol, defined separately in RFC 7664. At its core, dragonfly works by having both sides derive a secret group element (called the Password Element or PE) from a password, then each side makes a cryptographic commitment to its PE using randomly generated secret values.

The key innovation is hunting and pecking: because a password is low-entropy, it cannot be used directly as a group element. Instead, both sides iterate a hash function with a counter until they find a valid group element that can serve as the PE. To prevent side-channel attacks that count iterations, a security parameter forces at least m iterations to always be performed, even after the PE is found.

Once each side has computed its commitment (a scalar and group element), they exchange these values and compute a shared secret using the other side's values and their own private information. If both sides used the same password, they derive the same shared secret and can authenticate the connection with TLS Finished messages. If they used different passwords, the derived secrets differ, and the exchange fails.
sections.eli5: Both sides secretly cook up a magic number from the password using lots of iterations (so no one can spy on how long it takes). Then they each send a proof they know their magic number, without sending the number itself. If both passwords were the same, they can make the same encryption key.

sections.title: Integrating with TLS Versions
sections.content:
TLS-PWD supports both pre-TLS 1.3 (TLS 1.2 and earlier) and TLS 1.3 with slightly different integration patterns.

In TLS pre-1.3, the password-based exchange uses the ServerKeyExchange and ClientKeyExchange messages. The client sends its username (optionally encrypted for privacy) in a ClientHello extension. The server responds with its commitment and the domain parameters in ServerKeyExchange, including the salt (if the password was salted). The client sends its commitment in ClientKeyExchange. Both sides then compute the premaster secret from the shared group element, and TLS continues normally with ChangeCipherSpec and Finished messages.

In TLS 1.3, the password exchange is more streamlined. Both the client's and server's commitments go into the key_share extension, which TLS 1.3 already supports for key exchange. The client includes a pwd_name extension for its username. If the password is salted on the server, the server sends the salt back in a HelloRetryRequest before proceeding.

The RFC defines four ciphersuites, all using elliptic curve cryptography: TLS_ECCPWD_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_ECCPWD_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_ECCPWD_WITH_AES_128_CCM_SHA256, and TLS_ECCPWD_WITH_AES_256_CCM_SHA384. Implementations MUST support the first; others are RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: In older TLS, the password proof goes in special messages before encryption starts. In TLS 1.3, it fits into the normal key-sharing messages. Either way, once both sides agree on a shared secret from the password, TLS encrypts the rest normally.

sections.title: Group Operations and Cryptographic Support
sections.content:
TLS-PWD supports two families of discrete logarithm groups: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) and Finite Field Cryptography (FFC), each requiring different mathematics for hunting and pecking.

For ECC groups, the hunting-and-pecking algorithm generates a candidate x-coordinate, checks whether it lies on the curve (by solving y^2 = x^3 + ax + b), and if so, selects a y-coordinate consistently using a random seed. The search continues with a fresh random base value until the security parameter m has been reached, masking timing information from attackers.

For FFC groups (finite field cryptography), the algorithm instead exponentiates candidate values by (p - 1)/q to check whether they generate valid group elements, and continues until the security parameter is satisfied.

A compliant implementation MUST support ECC group 23 (NIST P-256) and SHOULD support group 24 (NIST P-384) or FFC groups 256 and 258. All ECC curves MUST be over prime fields (GF(p)) and have co-factor one; characteristic-2 curves and curves with larger co-factors are forbidden due to side-channel vulnerabilities.
sections.eli5: The password magic number must be a valid point on a chosen curve (elliptic curve math) or a valid element in a prime field (traditional Diffie-Hellman). The code iterates until it finds one, padded with extra work to hide how long it takes.

sections.title: Username Protection and Salt Management
sections.content:
TLS-PWD supports optional username protection, allowing the client's username to be encrypted before transmission. This prevents passive eavesdroppers from learning who is authenticating, and thwarts active attacks where a malicious server tries to determine if a username exists.

To enable protection, the server generates an ephemeral public/private keypair and publishes its public key to clients at provisioning time. When a client connects, it performs a static-ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange with the server's public key, derives a symmetric encryption key using HKDF, and encrypts the username with AES-SIV (a deterministic authenticated encryption cipher). The encrypted username and the client's public key are sent in the ClientHello. The server decrypts by performing the same computation on its side.

Passwords can optionally be salted on the server: the password-derived base (used to compute the PE) becomes HMAC-SHA256(salt, username | password) instead of a simple hash. When a password is salted, the server sends the salt in ServerKeyExchange (TLS pre-1.3) or HelloRetryRequest (TLS 1.3), and the client recomputes the PE with the salt before continuing.
sections.eli5: The username can be encrypted so eavesdroppers don't learn who is logging in. Passwords can have salt added so a stolen password database can't be pre-computed. The server sends the salt if needed, and the client regenerates the magic number with it.

sections.title: Dictionary Attack Resistance and Threat Model
sections.content:
The fundamental security guarantee of TLS-PWD is resistance to offline dictionary attacks. An attacker who captures a TLS-PWD handshake or even the entire TLS 1.3 ClientHello cannot take it offline and test password guesses. Why? Because the protocol commits both sides to a single password guess before any verification occurs.

In TLS pre-1.3, an active attacker impersonating the server sends a ServerKeyExchange with its commitment using a guessed password. If the guess is wrong, the client will compute a different PE, leading to a different shared secret and failed authentication at the Finished message. The attacker gets one active guess per attack.

In TLS 1.3, the same principle holds: the client sends its commitment in the ClientHello, and the server's Finished message implicitly verifies whether the server used the same password. A Finished message cannot be forged without knowledge of the shared secret derived from the correct password.

The security parameter m (the number of hunting-and-pecking iterations) is critical: it provides timing resistance against side-channel attacks. The RFC recommends m ≥ 40, which makes the probability of requiring more than 40 iterations approximately 1 in 1 trillion for large groups.

A password database compromise is serious: the stored base (password-derived value) must be treated as a plaintext password database. However, short passwords like four-character lowercase strings provide security through the interaction model: an attacker with a small password pool would need tens of thousands of active attacks to achieve advantage, which is easily detected by rate-limiting countermeasures.
sections.eli5: An eavesdropper can't guess passwords offline because each guess requires actually talking to the server and getting caught. Even if someone steals the password database, they can't speed up guessing beyond one try per real connection attempt.
